entry.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4B-parameter looped transformer model optimized for local laptop use and agentic reasoning tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Thinking Machines has launched Inkling 2 Mini, a compact looped transformer model with 26.4 billion parameters designed to run efficiently on consumer laptops and desktops. The model applies its middle layers multiple times per token to enhance reasoning quality, outperforming other open-weight models under 100 billion parameters on benchmarks like DeepSWE v1.1 and Vals Index v2.2, while maintaining a memory footprint of about 20GB. Inkling 2 Mini excels in agentic coding and long-horizon reasoning tasks, leading similar-sized models on several benchmarks and demonstrating improved performance with increased looping passes. It balances reasoning capabilities with efficient energy use, making it suitable for running multiple persistent AI agents locally. However, it is less effective on multi-turn chat and instruction-heavy tasks compared to larger models. The model is available with open weights on the Tinker platform for inference and customization.

entry.title: Researchers demonstrate a 27B parameter language model that rewrites its own weights to improve accuracy without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A new study shows that a large language model can self-optimize by rewriting its own weights through reasoning, improving its accuracy on unseen problems by 6.6 points without gradient updates or additional training. The model tests its edits iteratively, only applying changes that enhance performance, and can repair a damaged copy of itself to regain over 80% of original accuracy on image tasks it never encountered before. This self-rewriting ability emerges only at larger scales and operates solely through forward passes, blurring the line between training and inference. The researchers suggest this approach could enable continuous self-improvement without external retraining or prompt engineering.

entry.title: Anthropic shares fall 12% on second trading day amid AI sector sell-off, dragging Nasdaq down and wiping out 2026 gains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic's shares dropped by as much as 12% on their second day of trading, falling close to their IPO price, as a broader sell-off in AI-related stocks pressured the Nasdaq and other technology indices. The initial surge in Anthropic's stock on its debut was followed by a sharp decline, reflecting investor concerns about valuations and profitability in the AI sector. The sell-off extended globally, with Asian markets experiencing their worst week since 2020, led by declines in major chipmakers and tech investors like SoftBank. Analysts noted that Anthropic's IPO may have drained liquidity from other tech stocks as investors reallocated funds. The downturn also coincided with regulatory scrutiny of companies like Nvidia and broader market worries about interest rate hikes and inflation. This market turbulence highlights growing skepticism about the sustainability of heavy investments in AI and technology, as investors question whether these companies can deliver the expected returns amid elevated valuations and economic uncertainties.

entry.title: Engineer uses AI coding agents to program an FPGA for running a large language model, achieving a 33× speedup to 213 tokens per second [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: An engineer experimented with programming an FPGA to run a large language model (LLM) using AI coding agents, achieving a significant performance improvement. By leveraging cloud-based FPGA instances and AI models like Codex, Astra, and Opus, the project progressed from initial functionality to real-time inference speeds with minimal direct human coding. The process involved running extensive automated experiments over several days, generating millions of lines of code and output analysis while spending around $10,000 on AI tokens. The engineer combined AI-driven code generation with occasional expert guidance, resulting in a 33-fold speed increase from the baseline to 213 tokens per second. This work demonstrates the potential of AI-assisted development for hardware programming and AI inference acceleration on reprogrammable chips.

entry.title: Opinion: Concerns Raised Over Anthropic's AI Development and Calls for Caution in Engagement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The article discusses ethical and safety concerns related to Anthropic, an artificial intelligence company, highlighting potential risks associated with its AI technologies. It urges caution in interacting with Anthropic's products and initiatives due to these unresolved issues. The piece emphasizes the need for careful regulation and oversight as the company prepares for significant developments in the AI sector.

entry.title: Researchers develop PsyWorld, a profile-conditioned state world model using transition-informed representations to improve human behavior prediction and generalize to unseen individuals
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced PsyWorld, a profile-conditioned state world model that integrates stable psychometric traits with observed environment-behavior state transitions to enhance human behavior prediction. Unlike traditional models that condition actions solely on static profiles, PsyWorld uses transition-informed representations learned through a posterior encoder and prior predictor to better capture behavioral dynamics. Evaluations in simulated environments with participant-disjoint splits demonstrated high accuracy and improved generalization to unseen individuals, establishing the value of transition supervision in behavioral modeling without implying causal psychological mechanisms or long-term state calibration.

entry.title: Researchers introduce LR-Merge to predict and correct interference in multi-task model merging using directional derivatives and surrogate affine models, improving efficiency and accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A new study presents LR-Merge, a method that predicts and corrects interference when merging separately fine-tuned models by evaluating first-order directional derivatives at the receiver model. This approach reduces computational costs by optimizing merge coefficients without backpropagation and improves performance across various base mergers, especially as more tasks are combined. The method outperforms alternatives relying on pretrained responses and matches the accuracy of exact teacher matching with lower compute requirements. LR-Merge uses a surrogate affine model to efficiently handle coefficient and task-subset queries, enabling faster and more scalable multi-task model merging.

entry.title: Researchers propose Density Feedback Control to improve transferability and target density accuracy of generative sparse adversarial attacks on CNN and Transformer models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced Density Feedback Control (DFC), a method that dynamically adjusts the sparsity coefficient in generator-based sparse adversarial attacks to better achieve target perturbation densities and enhance transfer attack success rates. Unlike traditional fixed-coefficient approaches, DFC modifies the coefficient based on the difference between observed and target densities without changing the generator's architecture or loss function. Experiments demonstrate that DFC achieves target densities within one percentage point and improves attack success rates on CNN and Transformer models while perturbing fewer pixels. However, when attacks are restricted to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC does not consistently improve performance, indicating complex interactions between such restrictions and density feedback.

entry.title: Researchers propose PoolDPP, a determinantal point process method for diverse sampling from language models with theoretical guarantees and improved performance on text generation and reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced PoolDPP, a method that enhances diversity in language model outputs by sampling subsets of strings using determinantal point processes (DPPs), which balance item quality and repulsion between similar outputs. PoolDPP generates a candidate pool, reweights samples, and selects diverse subsets with theoretical bounds on its approximation quality. Empirical evaluations show that PoolDPP improves diversity and quality trade-offs in open-ended text generation, ambiguous text-to-SQL translation, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

entry.title: Study analyzes impact of feature reduction techniques on adversarial robustness of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal perturbation attacks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated how different feature reduction methods affect the adversarial robustness of various machine learning classifiers, including support vector machines, decision trees, random forests, multi-layer perceptrons, and k-nearest neighbors, using the APT dataset. The study compared principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information, measuring outcomes with accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation scores. Results showed that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally improved robustness more consistently, while other techniques had variable effects depending on the classifier and attack type.

entry.title: Researchers construct a near-quadratic sample compression scheme of size O(d² log² d) for all VC dimension d classes, proving the weaker sample compression conjecture [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The sample compression conjecture, a longstanding open problem in learning theory since the 1980s, posits that every binary concept class with VC dimension d admits a sample compression scheme of size proportional to d. While the original conjecture remains unresolved, researchers have now proven the weaker version by developing a sample compression scheme with size O(d² log² d). This result advances understanding of the relationship between simplification and generalization in machine learning by showing that predictors consistent with training samples can be defined using a polynomially bounded subset of the data.

entry.title: Researchers propose HapBO, a Bayesian Optimization method using expert natural language priors compiled into reusable belief functions, improving sample efficiency without in-loop LLM calls [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce HapBO (Harnessed α-π Bayesian Optimization), which converts expert knowledge expressed in natural language into structured belief functions to guide Bayesian Optimization (BO). HapBO applies these beliefs as bounded multipliers on acquisition functions, preserving optimization performance without requiring repeated large language model (LLM) calls during the process. The method supports rich belief representations beyond Gaussian assumptions and maintains regret bounds even under adversarial beliefs. HapBO was evaluated on 40 HPOBench tasks, synthetic benchmarks in 6-15 dimensions, and real-world problems including cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. It achieved the lowest aggregate regret on HPOBench and improved outcomes in real-world tasks with query budgets of 12-20, while incurring minimal wall-clock time and token costs compared to other LLM-based approaches.

entry.title: Researchers release a long-range video face presentation attack detection dataset spanning 1-100 meters with two sensor types and benchmark CNN models for three-class classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced a new video-based face presentation attack detection (PAD) dataset comprising over 374,000 frames from 261 individuals captured at distances from 1 to 100 meters using a DSLR camera and a mobile sensor. The dataset includes three-class labels-live, spoof, and props (occlusions)-and is designed to address challenges in multi-distance capture and diverse environmental conditions that current PAD systems, typically limited to close-range detection, do not cover. Four convolutional neural network architectures were fine-tuned and benchmarked, with EfficientNet achieving the highest accuracy of 98.48% and an ACER of 2.01%.

entry.title: discoCVI package releases memory-efficient R implementation of DISCO index for density-based clustering evaluation, achieving up to 138x speedup and linear memory growth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The discoCVI package introduces a new R implementation of the DISCO internal cluster validity index, designed for density-based clustering and noise label evaluation. This version computes the index using the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, reducing memory usage to grow linearly with data size while maintaining quadratic runtime. Benchmarks show the implementation is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous R version for datasets of 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for up to 8,000 points, using significantly less memory and scoring 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with under 200 MB of memory.

entry.title: Researchers audit DeepMind's GraphCast weather model using sparse autoencoder features to test causal relevance and improve extreme-event forecasts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed internal representations of DeepMind's GraphCast, an autoregressive weather forecasting model, to determine if causal relevance requires physical semantics. They applied interventions to the model's internal activations during rollout to assess the impact on forecast accuracy, particularly for extreme events like tropical cyclones. Ablating a feature tied to the model's computational mesh increased global geopotential height error despite lacking clear physical meaning, while manipulating features associated with convection and low-level vorticity affected tropical cyclone intensity predictions. Amplifying convection-related features reduced intensity error by a median of 51% across seven storms. These findings distinguish physical interpretability from causal utility and demonstrate that sparse features can serve as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening in learned weather dynamics.

entry.title: Researchers develop coupled neural operator framework for temporal extrapolation of elastic seismic wave propagation in layered media with stress conditioning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed a coupled neural operator framework combining a time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network and a Fourier Neural Operator to predict seismic velocity fields beyond training intervals in layered elastic media. The model uses a predictor-corrector approach with reference velocity and stress fields to autoregressively forecast horizontally polarized shear waves in layered soil columns with varying depths and properties. Evaluations show the model reproduces key velocity arrivals and depth-dependent responses with mean normalized root-mean-square errors between 0.53% and 2.82% over extrapolation intervals. While the framework demonstrates effective temporal velocity prediction under stress conditioning, autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.

entry.title: Researchers propose a rate-distortion framework for hierarchical content summarization to quantitatively assess generative model performance in long-context question-answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a framework inspired by Shannon's rate-distortion theory to formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem. This approach extracts semantic hierarchies from source content to measure the trade-off between compression efficiency and information loss during generative content manipulation, enabling benchmarking of models based on rate budgets. The framework is demonstrated through experiments with state-of-the-art large language models on long-context question-answering tasks, providing insights into their efficiency and comprehension. Additionally, the semantic hierarchy guides retrieval-augmented generation, improving rate-distortion performance compared to existing baselines.

entry.title: Researchers develop Bayesian κ-Explorer for minimax transition estimation in unknown MDPs, simplifying exploration with Dirichlet priors and achieving comparable convergence rates to frequentist methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Bayesian κ-Explorer, an algorithm for active exploration in minimax transition estimation within unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs). By applying Dirichlet priors to transition distributions, the method simplifies the exploration process by using the posterior mean model and eliminating the need for confidence-set optimization, while maintaining a surrogate convergence rate of approximately T^{-1/3} similar to frequentist κ-Explorer. The approach leverages the posterior expected squared ℓ2 error equaling total posterior variance to provide a closed-form exploration signal. The team also establishes bounds on the maximum posterior variance relative to the optimal asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark. Experimental results on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi environments demonstrate that Bayesian κ-Explorer achieves lower worst-case transition-estimation errors compared to baseline methods.

entry.title: Researchers propose DualSAE framework to separate interpretability and reconstruction in sparse autoencoders, improving reconstruction fidelity by 29% and interpretability by 34% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce DualSAE, a modular framework that augments traditional sparse autoencoders with a Residual Branch to separate semantic interpretability from reconstruction fidelity. The Sparse Branch captures dominant semantic features, while the Residual Branch models non-semantic information, with a decorrelation loss minimizing overlap between them. DualSAE uses a two-stage training strategy and demonstrates improvements across vision and language datasets. The approach enhances downstream tasks such as topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and large language model steering by providing more interpretable representations without sacrificing reconstruction quality.

entry.title: Researchers introduce InflEns, a game-theoretic mixture of LoRA experts that uses training data allocation to predict expert specialization and guide inference without explicit gating [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present InflEns, a framework that models expert training and routing as a location game in a fixed prompt-trait space, allowing the allocation used for training to predict which expert performs best on a given prompt. Evaluated on seven safety-related benchmarks, InflEns shows that the expert with the highest share of prompts achieves the lowest negative log-likelihood on about 90% of prompts, outperforming random allocation and matching learned gating methods without training an explicit gate. The fixed routing mechanism enables tracing harmful behavior to individual experts, allowing targeted retraining that significantly reduces attack success rates while maintaining instruction following. InflEns offers controls over expert specialization through kernel choice, trait-space geometry, and expert count, and is designed as a general framework extendable to any encoder and data distribution.

entry.title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.

entry.title: {\phi}TD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.

entry.title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. We study products of permutations of five items, a task that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve on all input lengths under the standard conjecture that $\mathrm{TC}^0 \ne \mathrm{NC}^1$. On two-event windows, a 27B model answered 3 of 100 correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 when it generated intermediate steps. A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each. The same package passed 298 of 299 new windows on a fresh machine, missing the target of 0.99 for the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. A separate follow-up sized to allow one failure yielded 472 of 473. On 1,000-event room-swap documents, three of ten models solved all five documents by reasoning alone. All seven models tested both ways at this length solved all five with extraction and the register, with no chain of thought requested. With concurrent extraction, median wall-clock time fell from 136.1 to 10.4 s for Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s for GPT-6.1 Sol. At fixed per-token rates, mean cost per document fell by 55% for Sonnet 5.5 and 44% for GPT-6.1 Sol. A regular expression with an executor also solved all 15 fixed-format documents. On 500 free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader identified the recorded value in 68.8% of cases, compared with 61.0% for a frequency baseline fitted on the same training projects.

entry.title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.

entry.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.

entry.title: Process-Knowledge-Guided Latent Diffusion for Generative Design of Porous Architectures: A Case Study in Aerosol Jet Printing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Printed porous layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the layout that uses the material best depends on how the process settings shape the deposit. Generative models propose layouts quickly, but a generator that does not receive the process setting samples from the same distribution at every setting, even when the process-dependent score ranks candidate layouts differently. This paper examines whether process knowledge can steer a latent diffusion generator toward layouts suited to a given process setting in a prescribed design domain. We formulate a process-dependent utilization score in which a process model sets the length over which the utility of printed material decays with distance from a channel. The generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent representation, a topology U-Net, a ControlNet domain branch, and a separately trained regressor that predicts the score from noised latents; the domain branch conditions each denoising step and the regressor gradient steers it. The method is applied to aerosol jet printing, where the atomizer and sheath gas flows enter the score through the flow-focusing relation. Across seven modeled flow settings, the lowest-scoring candidate layout of a domain differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains. In a sampling study, the mean directly computed score on three validation domains and one test domain was 0.642 with domain conditioning alone, 0.636 at a weight of 300, and 0.450 at 12,000 (112 scores per weight; lower is better). The results support process-knowledge-guided generation as an approach to process-specific porous design under the stated assumptions.

entry.title: Learning to Verify: Signature-Guided Training for Adaptive Adversarial Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial example detectors often fail when attackers explicitly attempt to bypass them. We propose a dual-model approach that keeps the original classifier fixed and trains a separate verifier to assess its predictions. During training, we identify patterns of internal neural network activations that distinguish genuine examples of each class from adversarial examples targeting that class. These patterns, called activation signatures, guide the generation of challenging adversarial examples that mislead the classifier, challenge the verifier, and internally resemble the target class. The verifier learns to recognize these examples while preserving its performance on clean inputs through knowledge distillation. At inference, the verifier evaluates the classifier's prediction without requiring activation signatures. We evaluate the approach on publicly available datasets against several adaptive attacks, including attacks unseen during training. The proposed verifier substantially outperforms directly attacked confidence-based and feature-based detectors under the evaluated L-infinity attacks. Ablation studies show that adaptive verifier training is the main source of this improvement, while signature guidance primarily benefits clean accuracy. Additional L2 evaluations reveal limitations in robustness across perturbation types.

entry.title: Scone: Symmetry-aware Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Graph Coloring [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph coloring, which entails assigning colors to nodes such that no adjacent nodes have the same color, is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem. In general, however, finding a node coloring with no monochromatic edges given a fixed palette is NP-hard. This motivates learning-based methods that can learn to exploit recurring structure across instances to efficiently produce high-quality colorings. Crucially, the validity of a coloring is invariant to permutations of the colors, and we show that exploiting this symmetry reduces the size of the effective state space over which the model has to learn its policy. At the same time, the coloring algorithm must be able to break some symmetries, for example to assign different colors to two adjacent nodes belonging to the same automorphism orbit. In this paper, we introduce Scone, a model that uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to construct colorings sequentially, allowing information from previous assignments to propagate and break node symmetries. Scone achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks, including on sudoku_extreme and register allocations, and showcases generalization to graph families not encountered during training.

entry.title: DS3M: Deep structured state space models for nonlinear system identification on modern hardware [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

entry.title: Intelligent Embedding Pruning for Large-Scale Recommendation Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.

entry.title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.

entry.title: Federated Learning of Car Aerodynamics Surrogates with Spectral Optimizers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural surrogates predict the aerodynamic forces on a car in seconds, compared with hours for a CFD simulation, but training them requires thousands of CFD simulations of different car designs, which car manufacturers keep proprietary. Federated learning allows several manufacturers to train a shared surrogate without exchanging data. We study which federated optimizer brings such a surrogate closest to one trained on pooled data. On DrivAerNet++, we train a Transolver surrogate across six clients that each hold cars of a single body type, and we compare three spectral optimizers, which orthogonalize the update of each weight matrix (FedMuon and two methods we propose, FedMARS-M and FedOLion), with three non-spectral ones (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam and FedLion), all tuned with the same protocol. FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized training with Muon, using two to four local epochs per round. The non-spectral methods perform best with sixteen local epochs, the largest number we tested, and still have a 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M. We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step yields about twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm. Code: https://github.com/armanbolatov/fedmars_drivaernet

entry.title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.

entry.title: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25320v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.

entry.title: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In regulated domains such as lending, the two most salient fairness concepts are disparate impact and disparate treatment: disparate impact is generally defined by differential rates of adverse outcomes between demographic groups, while disparate treatment is generally defined by the use of demographic information or proxies to issue decisions. There already exist established methods to quantitatively detect and mitigate disparate impact; however, there has been less research on doing the same for disparate treatment. From a practitioner's perspective, the manner in which a conditional independence test is formulated and operationalized to identify proxies is nuanced and underexplored. As Machine Learning (ML) systems increase in scope and application in regulated domains, practitioners need a defensible framework to identify proxies at scale. Current disparate treatment frameworks typically rely upon some combination of quantitative and qualitative review of models' inputs to identify proxies. Features that are identified as proxies are then typically removed from the model in practice, and predictive performance degrades in favor of fairness through unawareness. Here, we propose a two-part framework that reduces the disparate treatment risk of a feature and keeps the predictive performance that removal of the feature loses. First, we propose a quantitative test for proxy capacity that identifies whether some of a feature's values reveal membership in a particular demographic group. Second, we propose a pre-processing methodology that adjusts those proxy features to reduce their proxy capacity. We show empirically on synthetic and public datasets that this framework identifies features that proxy for demographic information and reduces their proxy capacity while the adjusted feature retains task-relevant signal (i.e. improves predictive performance versus removal).

entry.title: Class-Conditional Conformal Triage for ICAO Face-Image Compliance under Class Imbalance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated ICAO/ISO face-image compliance analysers provide criterion-level pass/fail decisions, yet these verdicts do not quantify uncertainty when deciding whether to accept, reject, or retake a photograph. We investigate conformal prediction as a triage layer for BioGaze, evaluating 14 compliance criteria on the synthetic TONO benchmark. Without retraining the analyser, we fit per-criterion logistic classifiers and compare marginal and label-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction with conventional abstention rules using subject-disjoint splits. Marginal conformal prediction achieved approximately 0.90 overall coverage but substantially under-covered violations, with a ten-partition mean of 0.37 for one criterion. The corresponding Mondrian means ranged from 0.89 to 0.92 across criteria. However, most of the reduction in criterion-level false positives came from the logistic layer (0.145 to 0.048), while tuned abstention rules achieved lower false-positive rates than Mondrian at comparable retake rates. Bonferroni correction for joint coverage across 14 criteria required retaking nearly all images. These findings show that class-conditional conformal prediction can achieve near-target empirical coverage for minority violation classes and reveal trade-offs between statistical coverage, classification performance, and retake requirements in multi-criterion face-image compliance assessment.

entry.title: Drifting, Discriminating, and Directioning for Action Coordination in Higher-dimensional Action Space [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a lightweight policy model to mitigate the difficulty of handling higher-dimensional action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL), alongside an algorithm to effectively train it. To address this, we focus on drifting models, which can implicitly represent complex distributions and infer actions in a single forward pass. However, while drifting models can be straightforwardly trained via backpropagation of the Q-gradient, this alone cannot be expected to appropriately capture the desired action coordination. Therefore, this paper constructs a three-step learning algorithm to encourage the action coordination. First, the source distribution of the drifting model is co-optimized as a diagonal policy model. This conditions the drifting model to attach the coordination, which cannot be expressed by a diagonal distribution, as residuals. Second, a discriminator model before and after drifting is introduced with adversarial training for a regularization term. This actively promotes the extraction of the coordination that fundamentally separates the two distributions. Third, best-of-N sampling is applied for action selection during rollouts in order to give directionality toward/beyond the regions where the coordination is insufficiently extracted/sufficiently discovered. The proposed method consistently improves the sample efficiency and the final control performance over the conventional diagonal distribution modeling across three locomotion tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that this improvement is achieved by reducing variance in certain action dimensions, effectively coupling them with other actions as action coordination.

entry.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

entry.title: Protein Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are commonly pretrained with likelihood-based objectives such as masked language modeling or denoising. These objectives capture sequence-level regularities, but can produce representations in which functional signals are entangled with non-functional variation (e.g., sequence identity, compositional bias, and frequent local motifs), creating a readout bottleneck for downstream function prediction. We introduce Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification (SAVR), a contrastive post-training method using Pfam family co-membership as a homology-guided discrete semantic signal to reshape PLM representations. SAVR reduces directional dominance and redistributes variance across embedding dimensions, decreasing variance concentration, and increasing effective dimensionality of the embedding covariance spectrum. Without observing any task-specific labels during post-training, SAVR achieves state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks and competitive results on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks under frozen-backbone evaluation. These results suggest that homology-guided contrastive post-training can rectify PLM representation geometry and improve sequence-based protein function prediction.

entry.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

entry.title: FG-GraphBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding with Multimodal Scene Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to recognize small visual entities and understand their relationships. Scene graphs offer a natural way to represent this information, organizing visual entities as nodes and their relationships as edges. However, we identify two challenges: existing scene graph benchmarks provide insufficient coverage of fine-grained entities and the relationships among them, and existing methods for fine-grained visual understanding have yet to effectively leverage such graph-structured information in MLLMs. To address these challenges, we introduce Fine-Grained Multimodal Scene Graph Benchmark (FG-GraphBench) and FiGRA. FG-GraphBench is a benchmark comprising three complementary tasks: fine-grained visual question answering (FG-QA), image captioning (FG-Caption), and image description generation (FG-Description). We develop a two-stage construction pipeline that discovers and grounds fine-grained entities and establishes their relations to construct the fine-grained multimodal scene graphs (MSGs) in FG-GraphBench. Building on these MSGs, we propose FiGRA, a Fine-grained Graph Representation Augmentation method for MLLMs. FiGRA adopts a two-stage training strategy. It encodes multimodal entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens, and integrates them into the MLLM. Experiments show that FiGRA significantly outperforms strong baselines across three tasks of FG-GraphBench. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of FG-GraphBench and highlight the importance of preserving fine-grained entity and relation information for visual understanding.

entry.title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

entry.title: Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.25424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities.
